title: Proactive SLA Floor and Cross-Pool Spillover Throttle
author: Maya Chen
release_notes: Introduce proactive SLA floor controller to guarantee per-tenant throughput floors and a cross-pool spillover throttle that prevents noisy tenants from causing headroom collapse. Adds predictive workload classifier and new utilization exporter with percentile windows.
description: Context: We continue to see incidents where sudden tenant spikes exhaust warm pools and cause cascading latency SLO violations across dedicated pools. Existing reactive autoscalers and soft-reservation hedges are effective but respond after degradation has already begun. This PR implements a proactive SLA floor controller that maintains a short-term throughput floor for tenants approaching their SLO budget and a cross-pool spillover throttle that enforces graded backpressure when a tenant would otherwise cause systemic headroom collapse. Motivation: reduce tail latency incidents and improve availability by combining predictive signals with conservative reserved bandwidth. Design summary: 1) SLA Floor Controller: monitors per-tenant short-window utilization (1s/10s/1m histograms) and predictive classifier output; when a tenant is predicted to spike beyond its active headroom, the controller pins a transient throughput floor (tokenized micro-reservations) to a pool or warmlet set for the duration of the spike window. Floors are sized based on recent percentile throughput and an operator-configurable safety multiplier. 2) Predictive Workload Classifier: lightweight online model (feature set: req/sec trend, kv-cache hit ratio, mean token length, recent p50/p95 latency deltas) that emits a 30s spike-likelihood score. The classifier runs in the serving control plane and is intentionally conservative to avoid false positives. 3) Cross-Pool Spillover Throttle: when a tenant's projected demand would exceed remaining headroom across all pools, the throttle introduces a graded backpressure token that reduces enqueue priority or routes additional requests to an overflow path (degraded model variant or lower-cost pool) based on tenant tier. 4) Telemetry and Auditing: new utilization exporter exposes winsorized percentile metrics (p50/p90/p95/p99) over multiple windows (10s/1m/5m) and an event trail for reactive investigations. Implementation notes: - Controller implemented in orchestration/autoscaler/sla_floor_controller.go with unit tests and integration harness - Classifier implemented as a pluggable function in autoscaler/predictive/online_classifier.go; default is rule-based logistic estimator, with a simple feature normalizer. - Throttle implemented in routing/spillover_throttle.go with backward-compatible policy interface; existing routing fallbacks remain intact. - Telemetry exporter added under observability/exporters/tenant_util_percentiles.go; adds a new metrics namespace redwood.dedicated.utilization.percentiles. Checklist: - [x] Spec doc in Linear: ENG-4821 - [x] Unit tests for controller and throttle - [x] Integration tests in perf-canary with synthetic spike scenarios - [x] Backwards compatibility preserved (default feature flag off) - [x] Docs update draft in redwood-docs (link below) Testing and results: - Ran perf canary with three synthetic tenants (steady, bursty, noizy) across two pools. Compared baseline (no proactive floor) vs this branch. Observed 72% reduction in p99 latency spikes for non-noisy tenants during noisy tenant bursts, and 18% lower warm-pool churn. CPU overhead of classifier + controller ~2.3% at 10k rps. Rollout plan: feature-flagged rollout by customer cohort; enable in internal staging for 48h, gradual ramp to 10% of dedicated customers, then 50% over 72h, monitor p99 latency and warm-pool replenishment. Ops knobs: sla_floor.watermark (percentile basis), sla_floor.safety_multiplier, spillover.throttle_granularity, predictive.classifier_threshold. Backwards compatibility: all routing fallbacks and autoscaler behaviors preserved unless the feature flag is enabled. Security and cost: no new secrets. Slight additional control-plane CPU cost; no notable GPU or per-request cost. Documentation: draft changes in sources/github/redwood-docs/docs/dedicated/sla-floor.md and runbook in ops/playbooks/sla-floor-runbook.md Related: ENG-4890 (investigate headroom collapse), SUP-1287 (customer incident postmortem).

review_comments: Rohan Patel: Nice approach — can you clarify how we size floors when tenant history is sparse?
Maya Chen (author): We use a damped estimator that falls back to cluster median and a conservative multiplier; doc updated with formula and tests to cover sparse-history path.
Grace Lee: The classifier looks good but we should avoid DDoS amplification. Add a hard cap on pin duration and token count.
Maya Chen (author): Added hard caps (config: sla_floor.max_duration, sla_floor.max_tokens) and unit tests covering caps.
Omar Ruiz: Telemetry naming collides slightly with existing percentiles. Please use winsorized/prefix and add migration notes.
Maya Chen (author): Renamed metric namespace to redwood.dedicated.utilization.percentiles and added migration note in observability/UPGRADING.md.
